extracted.intended_audience: applicants seeking registration to practice before the USPTO (patent agents/attorneys), USPTO OED staff, and practitioners handling moral-character reviews
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of an applicant's good moral character and reputation for registration to practice before the USPTO under 35 U.S.C. §2 and 37 C.F.R. §11.7, including consideration of criminal conduct, substance use, rehabilitation efforts, and candor in disclosures. Applies to petitions for review of OED Director decisions under 37 C.F.R. §11.2(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory requirement: good moral character and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. §2(b)(2) the USPTO may require applicants to show they 'are of good moral character and reputation' before being recognized as representatives before the USPTO; 37 C.F.R. §11.7 implements this by refusing registration unless the individual 'possesses good moral character and reputation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a threshold eligibility requirement for registration to practice before the USPTO; the Director's stated duty is to ensure representatives act with 'the highest degree of candor and good faith' to protect the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant bears the burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner/applicant bears the burden of showing that he or she is of good moral character and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must provide evidence and explanations to satisfy the OED Director; mere assertions are insufficient. Failure to meet the burden supports denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: No new evidence on petition for review
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 C.F.R. §11.2(d) the USPTO Director will consider no new evidence when deciding a petition for review of an OED Director's final decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On administrative review to the Director, applicants may not introduce additional evidence not considered by OED; arguments must be based on the record before OED.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of 37 C.F.R. §11.7(i)(1)-(12) rehabilitation factors
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating rehabilitation and moral character, the OED Director considers the factors enumerated in 37 C.F.R. §11.7(i)(1)-(12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should address these specific factors in their submissions (the decision noted that the petitioner provided statements addressing each factor). The Director evaluates the totality of those factors to determine current good moral character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstinence requirement for substance-related misconduct (37 C.F.R. §11.7(j)(7))
rubrics_metrics.description: If specific misconduct was attributable in part to alcohol or controlled substance use, abstinence from use for not less than two years is required, where abstinence may be demonstrated by, but is not limited to, enrolling in and complying with a self-help or professional treatment program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completion or active, documented compliance with treatment/self-help programs is needed to demonstrate the two-year abstinence; mere partial or informal counseling sessions are insufficient. The decision cites lack of demonstrated two-year abstinence as a key deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion of court-imposed programs as evidence of rehabilitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fulfillment of court-imposed requirements (e.g., Alcohol Safety Action Program - ASAP) is relevant evidence of rehabilitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to complete court-ordered programs, absent convincing justification, weighs against a finding of rehabilitation and current good moral character. Moving jurisdictions without arranging completion is the applicant's responsibility and unfavorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recency of misconduct matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent misconduct undercuts a showing of current good moral character (citing In re Mustafa as an example where denial was based largely on recency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if sanctions were imposed or time has passed, misconduct that is too recent can justify denial; the Director considers how much time has elapsed and whether sufficient rehabilitation has been shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession/use of controlled substances is a violation regardless of provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession of a controlled substance without a valid prescription is a violation of law regardless of how the substance was obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimizing how the substance was acquired (e.g., obtained from a family member rather than a dealer) does not neutralize the legal violation and undermines claims of good moral character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimizing or disingenuous explanations undermine credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to excuse or minimize misconduct (claiming ignorance of illegality or downplaying conduct) are problematic and detract from assertions of responsibility and candor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations that appear evasive or inconsistent with admissions (e.g., admitting Ambien is prescribed yet claiming ignorance of illegality) reduce the persuasive value of the applicant's statement and support denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and candor in disclosures are critical
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants' honesty and candor in answering application questions and in responses to OED inquiries are central to the moral character assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full, accurate, and candid disclosure is expected; concealment or misleading statements are significant negatives. The decision emphasized that truthful disclosure to law school and employers, while relevant, may be insufficient without other rehabilitation evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters of support and institutional admissions are not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters (e.g., law school admissions letters, employer references) and evidence that an arrest record did not affect admissions/employment are considered but are of limited weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such documents may assist but will not override objective shortcomings (e.g., failure to complete treatment, recent misconduct, lack of abstinence). The Director may find them of 'little weight' if other factors indicate lack of rehabilitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative disciplinary outcomes are illustrative, not controlling
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations to other disciplinary cases with lesser sanctions are only examples and do not dictate the outcome because each case presents different facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should not rely on favorable outcomes in other cases as determinative; focus should be on addressing the regulatory factors and specific deficiencies in the applicant's own record.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED procedural mechanisms: requests for information and Show Cause orders
rubrics_metrics.description: OED may request additional information about application answers and may issue a Show Cause Requirement to require the applicant to explain why registration should not be denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must timely and fully respond to such inquiries and Show Cause orders with substantive evidence and explanations addressing the regulatory factors; inadequate responses risk denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision review standard: Director will affirm if record supports OED
rubrics_metrics.description: On petition for review, the USPTO Director will affirm the OED Director's decision if it is supported by the record and the statutory/regulatory standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because no new evidence is considered on review, applicants should ensure the record before OED fully addresses all relevant factors; a well-documented showing of rehabilitation must be presented to OED initially.
